The docstring for the @[congr] attribute very explicitly mentions that lemmas marked with this attribute should vary all parameters.

@[congr] docstring

Registers `simp` congruence lemmas.

A `simp` congruence lemma should prove the equality of two applications of the same function from
the equality of the individual arguments. They are used by `simp` to visit subexpressions of an
application where the default congruence algorithm fails. This is particularly important for
functions where some parameters depend on previous parameters.

Congruence lemmas should have an equality for every parameter, possibly bounded by foralls, with
the right hand side being an application of a parameter on the right-hand side. When applying
congruence theorems, `simp` will first infer parameters from the right-hand side, then try to
simplify each left-hand side of the parameter equalities and finally infer the right-hand side
parameters from the result.

Example:
```lean4
def Option.pbind (o : Option α) (f : (a : α) → o = some a → Option β) : Option β := ...

@[congr]
theorem Option.pbind_congr
    {o o' : Option α} (ho : o = o') -- equality for first parameter
    {f : (a : α) → o = some a → Option β} {f' : (a : α) → o' = some a → Option β}
    (hf : ∀ (a : α) (h : _), f a (ho.trans h) = f' a h) : -- equality for second parameter
    o.pbind f = o'.pbind f' := -- conclusion: equality of the whole application
  ...
```

Nevertheless, even an experienced user like myself failed to recognize this, and it caused some breakage which I had to fix (by writing a better congr lemma) in #43689. Moreover, it seems that Mathlib has a bunch of bad congr lemmas which would be affected by the same sort of bug as mentioned in that PR (TL; DR for those who don't click through: bad congr lemmas can cause norm_cast not to visit all subexpressions in a single pass, making two passes necessary to actually normalize casts).

As examples, but I'm sure there are more: docs#Finset.filter_congr, docs#Finset.fold_congr, docs#Set.image2_congr, docs#Set.image_congr, docs#Sym.map_congr, docs#Sym2.map_congr

Of course, we could fix all of these, but would it be better to add a check upon adding a congr lemma that it actually varies all arguments, and warn otherwise? Does this need a change in core?

would it be better to add a check upon adding a congr lemma that it actually varies all arguments, and warn otherwise

I'm always strongly in favour of automating checks we humans would otherwise have to do, especially for subtle ones!
(Maybe this belongs in #lean4 :shrug:)
#43692 contains a syntax linter that tries to address this. Claude wrote it with my prompting.
If someone with more linter knowledge would like to do it better from scratch, I'm open to jumping in to help out.
I don't quite understand what you mean by "all parameters". In the example lemma from the docstring, the parameter α of Option.pbind is not varied, and I think this is perfectly fine.
α is implicit in docs#Option.pbind, this is only a check for explicit arguments.
Do you mean that it is just a performamce issue in norm_cast or does it actually become non-idempotent?

Note that docs#cfc_congr' is currently one of the bad congr lemmas

module

public import Mathlib.Analysis.CStarAlgebra.ContinuousFunctionalCalculus.Basic

example {A : Type*} [CStarAlgebra A] (n m : ℕ) :
    cfc (fun x : ℝ ↦ (x : ℂ).re) ((n : A) + m) = cfc (fun x : ℝ ↦ x) ((n : A) + m) := by
  norm_cast
  norm_cast
#44093 (still working through CI) is addressing the remaining lemmas.
I don't think there is necessarily a problem with these @[congr] lemmas. I would rather expect that this is a bug in norm_cast.
But that still leaves a contradiction between the doc-string of the @[congr] attribute and existing congr lemmas in mathlib. How do you propose we resolve this?
Regardless of whether this is a bug in norm_cast (it may be, as it may be the case that it should .continue at a certain point instead of .done), these @[congr] lemmas I think are wrong.
I suppose you are right that the docstring says that the lemmas should be changed.

Well I wrote this piece of documentation and I honestly don't remember if this is how I expected this sentence to be interpreted; but regardless, I believe putting as many arguments into the congr theorem as possible does have an advantage in terms of performance for simp.

You see, the way simp works is that in each step it tries every applicable congruence theorem and continues with the result of the first one that makes progress; and if none applies it uses its default congruence algorithm.

If we then have an application f a b, a congruence lemma that only touches a and b reachable through default congruence and two simp lemmas a = a', b = b', the following thing happens:

  • In the first pass of simp we use the congruence lemma to rewrite a to a'
  • In the second pass of simp we try to use the congruence lemma but fail; then we try the default congruence algorithm and rewrite b to b'
  • In the third pass of simp we try to use the congruence lemma but fail; then we try the default congruence algorithm but fail

If the congruence lemma instead touches both arguments, this happens:

  • In the first pass of simp we use the congruence lemma to rewrite a to a' and b to b'
  • In the second pass of simp we try to use the congruence lemma but fail; then we try the default congruence algorithm but fail

So having a better congruence lemma gets rid of one simp pass. I'm not sure how big the performance impact really is here but I believe it is at least somewhat faster to have a better lemma here. But the more important problem is that if we only run one pass, then we only rewrite a to a' in the case of a "bad" congr lemma. That can happen explicitly by using the +singlePass option or when the post simproc returns .done. This is what happens with norm_cast here.
